ctx.x: But I think at this point we’ve talked about how you developed as a saxophonist, to some extent. We should backtrack and figure out how you suddenly in 1928 were already an arranger, and the process by which you learned that craft. First of all, what made you decide that you wanted to arrange? Was there something you weren’t hearing in the music that you felt you wanted to hear?
You mean something I can improve on? No, not at all. [laughter] No, just that I wished that I could just do what I was hearing and do what other people were doing, not

feeling that I could, of necessity, do any better. But gee, I don’t know. I’m not sure, but I think Archie Blyer [phonetic] had a lot to do with that, if the time is right, because we played a few of his arrangements, you know, the stock arrangements, and Arthur Lang [phonetic] and other people, I think, who . . . Bob Herring, Paul Weirich [phonetic]. What other names were there that were doing stock arranging? Jimmy Dale, Jack Mason. items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I guess, Jimmy Dale, Jack Mason ... these are the names I remember, and I used to layout the parts on the floor and study them.

ctx.x: Jack Mason, Jimmy Dale ... people like that who were doing those things at that time -- and I would just take the parts and lay them out on the floor, and you know, first, second trumpet and trombone, and the two tenors and the alto -- I think that's the way it used to be in those days, just three brass, and three rhythm, and I started arranging like that. I would arrange ...
